title: Trump supporters in Congress give a Capitol tour to Jan. 6 attackers
description_short: Trump supporters in Congress give a Capitol tour to Jan. 6 attackers
description_medium: On January 5, 2021, Republican lawmakers gave a Capitol tour to Trump supporters, some of whom were later linked to the January 6 attack, according to the cited reporting. Representative Steve Cohen later identified Lauren Boebert in a CNN interview, and video showed Stop the Steal organizer Ali Alexander among the visitors. The record does not establish that the tour was planned as reconnaissance or that its participants knew of an attack plan.
description_long: Reporting published after the January 6 attack described a Capitol tour given the previous day to a group of Trump supporters. The supplied account initially left the lawmakers unnamed, then noted that Representative Steve Cohen identified Lauren Boebert during a CNN interview on January 18. It also points to video showing Stop the Steal organizer Ali Alexander among the visitors. The reporting prompted questions about access to the building in the days before the attack, but the available record does not provide a complete list of attendees or establish what the tour covered. Calling it a “reconnaissance tour” reflects an allegation about its purpose, not a demonstrated finding that the visitors were preparing an attack. The record likewise does not show that Boebert or any other lawmaker knew of a plan to breach the Capitol or knowingly assisted the people who later attacked it. What it does document is a tour involving political supporters before January 6, later scrutiny of at least one lawmaker’s connection to the group, and video identifying other participants. The distinction matters: proximity and access raise questions, but do not by themselves prove coordination or intent.
notes: Replaced the unrelated militarization tags and subcategory with the Capitol tour and January 6 subjects described by the sources. The account distinguishes reported attendance from unproven intent or coordination.

title: Press Freedom Systematic Destruction Through Legal Intimidation and Media Targeting
description_short: Press Freedom Systematic Destruction Through Legal Intimidation and Media Targeting
description_medium: A 2024 report by the Committee to Protect Journalists describes risks to U.S. journalists from violence, online harassment, subpoenas and litigation. It notes unsuccessful defamation suits brought by Donald Trump or his campaign against major news outlets. The report supports concern about burdens on reporting and sources, but does not document a decade-long campaign to criminalize journalism or establish the broader claims in this entry’s title.
description_long: The Committee to Protect Journalists’ 2024 report surveys pressures that journalists could face during the U.S. election period, including violence, online harassment, subpoenas and lawsuits. It points to defamation cases brought by Donald Trump or his campaign against major news organizations and describes how litigation can consume resources and deter reporting, particularly for outlets with limited legal capacity. Those are concrete press-freedom concerns, but the supplied source does not provide the dated case list or evidence needed to support the entry’s sweeping account of hundreds of lawsuits, encouraged death threats, credential and security-clearance removals, or efforts to criminalize routine journalism. It also does not establish that press freedom was systematically destroyed. A grounded description can report the risks identified by the organization and its examples of litigation, while keeping the more expansive allegations unresolved. Further records would be needed to connect specific threats or government actions to Trump and to show their scale and consequences. As written, the title asserts a broad finding that goes beyond the evidence in the linked report.
notes: Needs context: The linked CPJ report describes election-period risks and unsuccessful defamation cases but does not substantiate the title’s claim of systematic destruction or the synopsis’s asserted scale of lawsuits, threats, criminalization, and government targeting.
Proposed correction: Retitle this entry around the specific litigation and journalist-safety risks documented in the CPJ report, or provide dated primary records for the broader campaign claims.
Replaced the unsupported populated long description with an evidence-bounded account.

title: Military Force Threats Against Domestic Political Opposition
description_short: Military Force Threats Against Domestic Political Opposition
description_medium: In a 2024 interview, Donald Trump said the National Guard or military could be used against people he called “the enemy from within.” Coverage also describes proposals to move troops to the border and involve the military in deportation operations. These reports document statements and proposed uses of force; they do not show an actual domestic deployment against political opponents or a Posse Comitatus violation.
description_long: During a 2024 interview, Donald Trump said that the National Guard or military could be used to deal with people he called “the enemy from within.” The remark raised concern because it contemplated military involvement against people Trump portrayed as domestic opponents. The supplied coverage also describes proposals to move troops to the southern border and use military resources in deportation operations. Those proposals are relevant to the broader debate over domestic military roles, but they are distinct from proof that troops were actually deployed against political opposition. The available reporting records public statements and plans under discussion; it does not document an order carrying out such a deployment, a resulting military operation against civilians, or a court finding that the Posse Comitatus Act was violated. A separate January 2025 report about possible force abroad concerns a different set of targets and does not establish domestic action. The supported account is therefore about the threat and proposed role Trump described, and the concerns those statements raised. It should not be read as evidence that martial law was imposed or that the military suppressed political opponents.
notes: Replaced unsupported claims of completed deployment, Posse Comitatus violation, and preparation for military rule with a sourced account of statements and proposals.

title: Trump: Elon Musk's PAC accused of scraping voter data in swing states
description_short: Trump: Elon Musk's PAC accused of scraping voter data in swing states
description_medium: During the 2024 campaign, Elon Musk’s America PAC ran ads directing voters in swing states to a “register to vote” page. Reporting said some users were asked for personal details but were not sent to a state registration site; the PAC’s privacy policy allowed information to be used for other activities or fundraising. Michigan officials said they were reviewing the effort, but the report did not establish a legal violation or explain what happened to the data.
description_long: In August 2024, reporting described online ads from America PAC, Elon Musk’s pro-Trump political action committee, that invited people in battleground states to register to vote. Some users who followed the link were instead asked to provide personal information and were not directed to a state registration portal. The PAC’s privacy policy allowed submitted information to be used for other activities or fundraising. Michigan officials said they were reviewing the effort, while the reporting quoted experts who did not identify a clearly violated law. This establishes that a political committee collected information through a registration-themed page and that its stated data-use terms were broad. It does not show what information the PAC ultimately retained, whether it transferred the data to the Trump campaign, or how the information was used. Nor does the report establish that voters were successfully registered through the page or that the collection was unlawful. The distinction is important: the presentation of the page and the committee’s privacy terms raise questions about voter-data handling, but claims of a confirmed transfer, deceptive intent, or illegal conduct require evidence beyond the report. The linked accounts leave those outcomes unresolved.
notes: Replaced generic political and unrelated tags with America PAC, voter-data privacy, and the people and institutions named in the reporting; retained the report’s stated limits on transfer and legal findings.

title: Military Domestic Deployment and Posse Comitatus Act Violation
description_short: Military Domestic Deployment and Posse Comitatus Act Violation
description_medium: The accessible linked analysis describes a Trump order directing Justice and Defense officials to expand military equipment available to local police and assess military support for crime prevention. It discusses proposed policing measures, not a deployment of active-duty troops for domestic law enforcement. The other linked report could not be retrieved, so the title’s claim of a Posse Comitatus violation remains unsupported.
description_long: The accessible Marshall Project analysis concerns a Trump policing order that promised legal support for officers and directed Justice and Defense officials to increase military equipment available to local police within 90 days. It also ordered an assessment of military and national-security resources that could support crime prevention. These provisions describe equipment, legal assistance and a review of potential support; the analysis does not say that active-duty forces were deployed to conduct immigration raids, suppress protests or target political opponents. The other linked article, from Politico, returned an access-denied response when checked, so its account could not be used to verify the title’s allegation. The supplied materials therefore do not establish a Posse Comitatus Act violation, martial law, or suspension of constitutional rights. They do support a narrower account of an executive order that sought to expand federal backing and military equipment for local policing while studying additional military support. Before this entry can be presented as an actual domestic deployment or statutory violation, it needs a source documenting the specific operation, the forces involved and the legal basis. The title currently goes beyond what the available reporting shows.
notes: Needs context: The accessible source describes a policing order and review of possible military support; the linked Politico article returned HTTP 403 and the available material does not document active-duty deployment or a Posse Comitatus violation.
Proposed correction: Narrow the entry to the policing order and its review of military support, or provide an accessible source for the alleged deployments and legal violation.
Replaced the unsupported populated long description with a bounded account of the accessible reporting.
